title: An Antarctic Island Looks Like a Skull, and Its Ice Is Telling a Story
summary:
Seen from above, Vega Island in Antarctica looks like a grinning skull gazing toward nearby Devil Island. Behind that spooky sight is a serious story about changing glaciers.

Vega Island lies in the Weddell Sea, east of the Antarctic Peninsula. A nunatak, a rocky peak rising above the ice, resembles an empty eye socket. A lateral moraine, a ridge left along the side of a glacier, outlines the mouth, and the Bahia del Diablo, or Devil's Bay, Glacier forms the lower jaw.

NASA satellite images, captured by the Operational Land Imager aboard Landsat 9, show the island in March 2025 and again in October 2026. In March 2025, snow blanketed the terrain. By October 2026, extensive sections were free of snow, leaving darker glacier ice exposed.

Glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College explained that unusually warm conditions during the winter of 2026, especially in June, contributed to the exposed ice. Relatively little fresh snow accumulated, and some snow was lost through sublimation, when ice turns directly into water vapor, and through strong winds.

"The winter season was no treat for these glaciers," Pelto said.

The lack of snow could matter as Antarctica moves into warmer months. Fresh snow reflects much of the sunlight that reaches it, while darker ice absorbs more solar energy and is likely to warm more quickly, potentially speeding up melting. Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would help in the short run, Pelto said. Continued melting could also change the island's appearance: "When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket."
why_it_matters: Antarctica's glaciers hold vast amounts of ice, so changes in snow cover there can speed melting and affect sea levels far beyond the island.

background_read: A glacier is a huge mass of ice that moves very slowly over land, shaping the ground as it goes.
Fresh snow is bright and reflects much of the sunlight that hits it, while darker ice absorbs more sunlight and warms up faster.
Satellites can photograph the same place at different times, so scientists can compare how much snow and ice is there.
When glaciers lose snow and melt faster, their shapes can change over time.
